https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgq5.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Rubio accused multiple Cuban figures targeted by the sanctions of engaging in "subversive anti-American activities" By Will Grant ,Â Cuba correspondent Â and Â Harry Sekulich Published 4 hours ago The US has imposed a new round of sanctions on Cuban officials and companies, Secretary of State Marco Rubio says. Nine state-owned mining, metal and building firms, the Ministry of Construction and officials connected to a Cuban-based international institute have been named in the latest tranche of economic sanctions. In a statement, Rubio accused various figures of "ferrying a new brigade of international sympathizers to Havana to network with regime officials" to coincide with the late former leader Fidel Castro's 100th birthday. Cuba has denounced all sanctions imposed by the Trump administration. Rubio said the figures targeted by the sanctions form "part of the regime's raison d'Ãªtre of exporting Marxism, racial resentment, and Communist violence across the world". Rubio continued: "Today's designations make clear that the Trump Administration will not tolerate the Cuban regime's efforts to fund its repression or continue its decades-long campaign of subversive anti-American activities." The leadership of the Cuban Institute of Friendship with the Peoples (ICAP) were targeted in the latest round of US sanctions. Founded in 1960 by Castro, the ICAP has traditionally been used by the Cuban government to foster ties with like-minded organisations around the world by hosting visiting groups of activists who also promote pro-Cuban government campaigns in their own countries. Rubio, however, accuses the group of "misleading and corrupting American citizens with lies, spy tradecraft and malfeasance". Among those to be targeted is the group's president, Fernando Gonzalez Llort, a member of a spy ring called the Cuban 5, who were part of a prisoner exchange during the Obama-era thaw with Havana. Havana's senior figures across the energy, financial and defence sectors are already subject to US sanctions. The country's tourism industry has also plummeted, a key source of income for the beleaguered government. Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno RodrÃ­guez condemned Rubio's announcement, writing on X that he was trying to "punish" Cuban companies and further "harm" the economy. RodrÃ­guez added it would prevent the government "from guaranteeing basic services to the population, which are already in a critical situation as a result of the blockade". The US has imposed an effective oil blockade on Cuba since the beginning of the year. With the island's aging electricity infrastructure heavily reliant on fuel imports, hospitals have resorted to using emergency generators. Lengthy and frequent power cuts have triggered rare protests in Cuba, where public dissent is typically punished with long prison sentences. Photograph: The Guardian NAZA Global release announced for acclaimed Gaza documentary NAZA Theatrical rollout across 56 territories planned for documentary about Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza before film will stream on Guardian website Catherine Shoard and Lorenzo Tondo Thu 24 Sep 2026 06.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 06.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google NAZA, the award-winning documentary from Israeli film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, is set to be released in cinemas in more than 50 countries before a digital global release on theguardian.com. The film, which the Guardian produced, premiered at the Venice film festival earlier this month, where it was met with a 25-minute standing ovation – a festival record. The documentary went on to win the special jury prize . ‘They know the house they are bombing is full of children’: NAZA’s directors on their devastating film about Israeli intelligence Read more After screenings in Bologna and at the San Sebastián film festival, the film will receive its North American premiere on Saturday at the New York film festival before opening four days later at the IFC Center in New York City. On 9 October it will expand to Los Angeles and other key US cities before a national rollout. A theatrical release in partnership with MK2 Films is also planned in 55 other territories, including the UK, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, Canada, Hong Kong, Brazil, Turkey, Thailand, France, Spain, Germany, Turkey, Central America and the Middle East. After its run in cinemas, the film will stream on the Guardian’s website, for free, as part of the news organisation’s commitment to the dissemination of independent journalism. “NAZA is grounded in rigorous journalism published over the past three years,” said Harry Davies, a Guardian investigations correspondent and one of NAZA’s producers. “But it is also a powerful piece of cinema that will soon be available on screens, large and small, around the world.” Documentary NAZA gets 25-minute standing ovation at Venice film festival premiere – video A number of distributors and cinemas in Israel have been offered the film, and the Guardian is exploring ways by which NAZA can be seen in the occupied Palestinian territories. From ovations in Venice to death threats in Israel: the extreme responses to NAZA documentary Read more The documentary reveals the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza. NAZA is a military acronym euphemistically used by Israeli intelligence to indicate the number of civilians that it expects will be killed in an airstrike. Shot at night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv, the film features interviews with 24 members of Israeli intelligence and military, granted on the condition of anonymity. The film builds on journalism first published by the Guardian, +972 Magazine, an Israeli-Palestinian publication, and Hebrew-language outlet Local Call between 2023 and 2025. In 2024, Abraham and Szor won the best documentary Oscar for No Other Land, along with their two Palestinian co-directors, Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal. Jonathan Glazer, the Oscar-winning film-maker of The Zone of Interest and Under the Skin, has executive produced, while his longtime collaborator, James Wilson of JW Films, also produced the film. The film won unanimously positive reviews at its premiere, but last week Benjamin Netanyahu and a number of senior military and far-right political figures called for the directors’ citizenship to be revoked, and accused them of “treason against the state” . The Israeli prime minister said he would seek new laws allowing the country to strip citizenship from people who “smear” Israeli soldiers and “defame” the state of Israel. Alongside the announcement, dozens of rightwing activists gathered outside Szor’s parents’ home . Police and border police officers were deployed at the scene. One protester called for the “death penalty for traitors” and demanded that the homes of the film-makers’ families be demolished. Speaking on Thursday, Abraham and Szor said: “We made this film out of a sense of obligation to use our position as Israelis to examine the systems behind the mass killing of Palestinian civilians for which our country is responsible. “The threats from the Israeli government to revoke our citizenship and the death threats do not change that and will not stop the film. We thank our colleagues for the solidarity and look forward to sharing NAZA all over the world very soon.” ‘This should be condemned by any thinking human’: film industry rallies behind NAZA directors Read more Last week, 43 local human rights organisations issued a joint statement urging Israeli authorities to stop what they described as incitement and threats against the film-makers, and not to prosecute either them or their sources. More than 1,500 Israeli film-makers have also signed a petition defending “freedom of expression and creation” and expressing solidarity with Szor and Abraham. Their sentiments have been echoed by a number of leading film-makers around the world, including Ken Loach, Joshua Oppenheimer, Paul Laverty, Laura Poitras, Nan Goldin, Richard Eyre and Hanif Kureishi. Oppenheimer, the US director of Oscar-nominated documentaries The Act of Killing and The Look of Silence, said, “The Israeli government is waging a full-scale intimidation campaign against film directors. I am appalled and enraged.” Explore more on these topics NAZA Film industry Venice film festival Gaza Jonathan Glazer No Other Land Palestine news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://enrsi.stvr.sk/articles/topical-i.text: President Peter Pellegrini represented Slovakia at the 81st UN General Assembly in New York this week. In his address, he stressed respect for international law, UN reform and conflict prevention, while also calling for international rules on artificial intelligence, particularly its use in military systems. At a UN Security Council meeting on Ukraine, Pellegrini called for the protection of civilians and critical infrastructure, de-escalation and renewed negotiations. Slovakia also promoted its bid for a non-permanent seat on the Security Council for 2028 and 2029. Foreign Minister Juraj Blanár (Smer-SD) also attended talks on the International Criminal Court, reaffirming Slovakia’s support for its independence and international law. Slovakia additionally presented its culture through the Slovaks in Concert event at New York’s Lincoln Center. Moreover, Former Foreign Minister and Former Prime Minister Robert Fico’s national security adviser Miroslav Lajčák also attended the UN General Assembly and was seen with the Slovak delegation. His presence drew criticism from the opposition because of his association to the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, although the President’s Office claims he was not an official member of the delegation and had only come to greet its members. Source: TASR, aktuality.sk

(Photo by Dana Kesnerova/Xinhua) BERLIN, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- Czechia's opposition parties will retain their majority in the Senate after securing five seats outright in the first round of elections for the upper house of parliament, according to preliminary results released early Sunday. The five winners include candidates from the Christian Democrats, the Mayors and Independents and other opposition parties. Under the Czech electoral system, one-third of the 81-member Senate, or 27 seats, are contested every two years. Candidates must win more than 50 percent of the vote in their respective constituencies to secure a seat outright in the first round. The three main opposition groups hold 37 of the 54 seats not up for election. With five more seats secured in the first round, the opposition has ensured a majority of at least 42 seats, leaving Prime Minister Andrej Babis' ruling coalition in the minority. In the nationwide municipal elections also held on Friday and Saturday, independent candidates and local groups won the majority of local council seats, while Babis' ANO party led in several major regional cities. ■ Voters wait in line to fill in their ballots at a polling station in Prague, the Czech Republic, Oct. 9, 2026.
